title: A Summer in Grand-Bassam
author: Léxi
desc: Nadia passe l'été chez sa tante à Grand-Bassam. Un garçon qui peint la mer, une lettre jamais envoyée.

chapters.t: The Old House by the Sea
p: Nadia doesn't want to go to Grand-Bassam. All her friends are staying in Abidjan for the summer. But her parents are travelling for work, so she must stay with Aunt Clémentine.
Aunt Clémentine lives in the old town, in a yellow colonial house with blue windows. The paint is falling off the walls, but the garden is full of flowers. From the balcony, you can see the sea.
"You will be bored, I know," says Aunt Clémentine with a smile. "Young people are always bored here. And then they never want to leave."
The first evening, Nadia sits on the balcony with her phone. There is no good network. She sighs and looks at the beach.
Down on the sand, a boy is sitting in front of a small easel. He is painting the sunset.
The next day, Nadia walks on the beach. The boy is there again, with his easel. She stops behind him. His painting is beautiful: the sea is purple and gold, and the waves look alive.
"You can come closer," he says without turning around. "The sea doesn't bite."
"How did you know I was here?"
"Your shadow is on my painting," he laughs.
His name is Yann. He is seventeen. He lives in Bassam all year, and he sells his paintings to tourists on Sundays. He wants to go to the art school in Abidjan, but it is expensive.
"And you?" he asks. "What do you love?"
Nadia opens her mouth. Then she closes it. Nobody has asked her this question before. Not her parents. Not her friends.
"I don't know," she says honestly. "Maybe writing. I write little poems. But I never show them to anyone."
"Then show them to the sea first," says Yann. "The sea keeps all secrets."
The days pass quickly now. Every morning, Nadia helps her aunt in the garden. Every afternoon, she goes to the beach.
Yann shows her the old lighthouse, the museum, the place where the fishermen bring their boats at six o'clock. Nadia reads him her poems, first very quietly, then with a stronger voice.
"Your words are like my colours," says Yann one evening. "You paint with words."
They sit on the sand until the stars come out. They talk about everything: their dreams, their fears, their families. Nadia forgets her phone. She forgets that she wanted to stay in Abidjan.
One night, Aunt Clémentine sees them from the balcony. She smiles a little sad smile.
"Be careful, my dear," she tells Nadia later. "Summer loves are like waves. They come, and then they go."
The summer ends too fast. Tomorrow, Nadia's parents come to take her home.
All night, she writes a letter to Yann. She writes everything she feels. That he is the first person who saw her really. That she doesn't want to forget this summer. That maybe this is love.
In the morning, she runs to the beach with the letter. But Yann is not there. His easel is not there. The beach is empty.
She waits for one hour. He doesn't come. Her parents' car arrives in front of the yellow house.
Nadia gives the letter to Aunt Clémentine. "If you see him… please."
In the car, she doesn't speak. She looks at the sea until it disappears.
Six months later, Nadia is in Abidjan. She writes more than ever. She even sends a poem to a competition.
One day, Aunt Clémentine calls her. "Go to the Plateau, to the new art gallery. Today. Don't ask questions."

Nadia goes. On the wall of the gallery, there is a big sign: *Young Painters of Côte d'Ivoire.* And in the middle of the room, there is a painting of a girl reading on a balcony, in front of a purple and gold sea.
Under the painting, there is a small card: *"Nadia" — Yann Koné. Student, École des Beaux-Arts.*
"I got the scholarship," says a voice behind her. "Your aunt gave me your letter. I read it a hundred times."
Nadia turns around. Yann is there, with paint on his fingers, like always.
"I was at the hospital that morning," he says. "My mother was sick. I'm sorry I wasn't on the beach."
Nadia doesn't know if she wants to laugh or cry. So she does both.
Aunt Clémentine was wrong, she thinks. Some waves come back.
